q: You are the lookout on this yacht. Where is your blind spot?
a: On the port bow, behind the genoa
o: On the starboard bow, to windward
Abeam to starboard, by the shrouds
Straight ahead, behind the mast
why: The genoa hides the leeward bow — on starboard tack that is to port, so look under it often.

q: You are motoring at 6 knots and keeping a careful watch ahead. How often do you look astern?
a: Regularly — fast boats come up from behind
o: Never — an overtaking boat must keep clear
Only when the skipper asks you to
Only at night, when lights show up
why: A lookout covers all round; fast ferries and RIBs overtake quickly and quietly.

q: You spot this ship. How do you report it to the skipper?
a: 'Ship at three o'clock, about two miles'
o: 'Ship at nine o'clock, about two miles'
'Ship at twelve o'clock, about two miles'
'Ship at six o'clock, about two miles'
why: Clock bearings count from your own bow: 12 is dead ahead, 3 is abeam to starboard.

q: You have been taking bearings of this ship. What do you tell the skipper?
a: Bearing steady and closing — risk of collision
o: No risk — the ship is holding a steady course
No risk while it is more than a mile away
Risk only once the bearing starts to change
why: A steady bearing on a vessel that is getting closer means you are on a collision course.

q: You check a yacht three times with the compass. What do you report?
a: Bearing changing — it should pass clear, keep watching
o: Bearing steady — there is a risk of collision
It will hit us — the helm must tack at once
Bearings tell you nothing about the risk
why: A clearly changing bearing usually means you will pass clear — but keep checking until it is past.

q: You are sailing towards this boat. Who keeps clear?
a: You do — a boat fishing comes first
o: The trawler — power gives way to sail
Neither — both turn to starboard
The smaller of the two boats
why: Rule 18: a sailing vessel keeps out of the way of a vessel engaged in fishing.

q: You see these lights. Which way is the vessel heading?
a: Crossing ahead of you from right to left
o: Crossing ahead of you from left to right
Coming straight towards you
Moving directly away from you
why: You see its red port side, so its bow points to your left; the white light shows it is under power.

q: At night you are motoring up behind a slower yacht to overtake it. What do you see of its lights?
a: One white light, low down
o: A red and a green light side by side
A green light only
A white light above a red one
why: From astern you see only the white sternlight; the sidelights are hidden from behind.

q: You see only these two lights, close together at masthead height. What are they?
a: A sailing yacht heading towards you
o: A motor boat heading away from you
A yacht lying at anchor for the night
A fishing boat working its nets
why: A masthead tricolour: red and green together mean a sailing boat is bows-on to you.

fig.note: Night · almost dead ahead, high up

q: A motor boat ahead of you gives one short blast on its horn. What is it telling you?
a: 'I am altering my course to starboard'
o: 'I am altering my course to port'
'I am operating astern propulsion'
'I doubt that you are keeping clear'
why: Rule 34: one short blast — altering to starboard; two — to port; three — going astern.

q: You are sailing across a ferry route, holding your course. The approaching ferry sounds five short, rapid blasts. What does it mean, and what do you do?
a: It doubts your intentions — tell the skipper now
o: It is turning to port — carry on as you are
It is going astern — carry on as you are
It is giving way to you — carry on as you are
why: Rule 34(d): five or more short blasts signal doubt or a warning — act at once.

q: In the harbour, a large motor yacht leaving the quay sounds three short blasts. What is it doing?
a: Its engines are going astern
o: It is turning to port
It is turning to starboard
It doubts what you are doing
why: Rule 34: three short blasts mean 'I am operating astern propulsion'.

q: This motor boat is closing on a steady bearing. Who should keep clear?
a: Usually the motor boat — power gives way to sail
o: You — a boat on your starboard side has priority
Neither — both boats turn to port
Whichever boat is going faster
why: Rule 18: a power-driven vessel keeps out of the way of a sailing vessel, with a few exceptions.

q: You are sailing faster than a yacht ahead on the same course and slowly catching it up. Who keeps clear?
a: You — the overtaking boat keeps clear
o: The yacht ahead — it must let you pass
Whichever boat is on port tack
The yacht with the bigger sails
why: Rule 13: an overtaking vessel keeps clear, whatever its type or tack.

q: You are motoring and this boat is coming straight at you. What should happen?
a: Both boats turn to starboard
o: Both boats turn to port
The smaller boat stops
You hold course; it turns
why: Rule 14: head-on under power, each turns to starboard and they pass port to port.

q: Your friend says the ferry must give way because you are sailing. What do you say?
a: No — in a narrow entrance we keep clear of it
o: Right — power always gives way to sail
Cross quickly ahead before it speeds up
Stop in the entrance and let it go round
why: Rule 9: a sailing yacht must not impede a big ship that can only use a narrow channel.

q: You are on night watch and need to check something on the chart. Which light do you use?
a: A dim red light
o: A bright white torch, briefly
The saloon lights, switched on fully
Your phone screen on full brightness
why: Red light keeps your night vision; white light can spoil it for many minutes.

q: You are watching this vessel at night. What has it done?
a: Turned towards you — it now heads straight at you
o: Turned away from you — it is now moving off
Stopped and dropped anchor for the night
Switched its engine off and set sail
why: Seeing both sidelights means its bow points at you — report it to the skipper at once.

fig.title: Night watch
lines: 21:10 — a white light above a green one
21:15 — a red light appears by the green

q: You see this group of lights. What do you tell the skipper?
a: A large ship crossing from right to left
o: Two small boats, one behind the other
A sailing yacht heading towards you
A large ship moving away from you
why: Two masthead lights mean a ship over 50 m; the lower one is forward, and red is its port side.

q: As lookout, how do you handle this motor boat?
a: Call the skipper now, with bearing and distance
o: Wait until it is close enough to be sure
Say nothing — power gives way to sail
Steer away yourself without telling anyone
why: Report early: a steady bearing means risk of collision, and the skipper needs time to decide.
